Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 86, verses 1–4:

﴿By the sky and the one who comes at night﴾. This sky by which Allah swears is the well-known one. It has been said that He meant rain, because the Arabs sometimes call rain "sky," but this is far-fetched. The word al-tariq (the one who comes at night) in the language means whatever comes at night (yatruq, i.e., arrives at night). Allah Himself explains it here as the piercing star (al-najm al-thaqib), which appears at night. The meaning of al-thaqib is the shining one or the elevated one. It has been said that He meant the class of stars in general; it has been said that it is the Pleiades (al-Thurayya), because it is the one the Arabs call "the star" (al-najm); and it has been said that it is Saturn (Zuhal).

﴿Indeed, every soul has a guardian over it﴾. This is the answer to the oath, and its meaning according to the majority (al-jumhur) is that every human soul has a guardian over it who records its deeds, namely the noble recording angels (al-hafazah al-malaikah). It is narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) in explanation of this verse that for every soul there are guardians from Allah who ward off harm from it, just as one wards off flies from honey, and if a person were left to himself for the blink of an eye, the calamities and the devils would snatch him away." If this hadith is authentic, then it is the one relied upon.

It is also read as lamma ʿalayha with the mim lightened (takhfif), and on this reading inna is the lightened form of the heavy inna, the lam is for emphasis, and ma is extra (za'idah). It is also read as lamma with the mim doubled (tashdid), and on this reading inna is negating (nafiyah), and lamma carries the sense of affirmation after negation.

﴿So let man look at what he was created from﴾. The alif of مِمَّ (mimma, "from what") was dropped because it is an interrogative, and its answer is ﴿created from a gushing fluid﴾ (khuliqa min ma'in daafiq). The semen (al-mani) was called "gushing water" (maa' daafiq) from al-dafq, meaning "propulsion." Some said it means "propelled" (madfuq), and that its owner is the one who truly propels it. Sibawayh said it is in the relative form, meaning "possessing propulsion" (dhu dafq). Ibn 'Atiyyah said it is valid for the water to be called gushing because some of it propels other parts of it. The purpose of the verse is to establish the Resurrection (al-hashr). It commands man to consider the origin of his creation so that he knows that the One who created him from gushing water is able to restore him. The connection of this passage to what precedes it is that when He informed us that over every soul there is a guardian (﴿over every soul there is a guardian﴾) who records its deeds, He alerted to the Resurrection, when every soul will be recompensed for its deeds.

﴿It emerges from between the loins and the ribs﴾. The pronoun in yakhruju (it emerges) refers to the water. Ibn 'Atiyyah said it may refer to man, but this is very far-fetched. Al-taraa'ib (the ribs, sing. tariba) are the bones of the chest. It was also said they are the extremities, like the two hands and two legs. It was said they are the essence of the heart, from which the child comes. It was also said they are the ribs beneath the spine. The first is the correct and well-known meaning in the language, and for this reason Ibn 'Abbas said: they are the place of the necklace, between the breasts of a woman. The meaning is the loins and ribs of the man and the loins and ribs of the woman. It was also said that it means the loins of the man and the ribs of the woman.

﴿Indeed He is able to return him﴾. The pronoun in innahu (indeed He) refers to Allah the Exalted, and the pronoun in rij'ihi (His returning him) refers to man. The meaning is that Allah is able to return man alive after his death, and the purpose is to establish the Resurrection (al-ba'th).

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 86, verse 9–13:

﴿On the day when the secrets are tested﴾. That is, the Day of Resurrection. "Sara'ir" (secrets) is the plural of "sarira," which is what a servant conceals in his heart of beliefs and intentions, and what he hides of deeds. "Tabla'uha" (their testing) means making them known and bringing them to light. It is narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that the secrets are faith, prayer, zakat, and the ritual bath from major impurity, and these are the greatest of them. That is why he singled them out for mention. The element governing "yawm" (day) is the word "rad'ahu" (will return him), meaning: He will return him on the day when the secrets are tested. An objection was raised concerning the separation between the two, and it was answered by the strength of the verbal noun in governing. It was also said that the governing element is "qadir" (able), and an objection was raised that this restricts the ability to that day, but this does not necessarily follow, because although the ability is absolute, God has informed us that the resurrection will indeed occur on that day. Those who avoided the two objections in the two earlier opinions said: the governing element is an implied verb from the meaning, its estimate being: He will return him on the day when the secrets are tested. All of this is according to the correct meaning of "rad'ahu." As for the other opinions, the governing element for "yawm" is an implied verb, its estimate being: remember.

﴿Then he will have no power, nor any helper﴾. The pronoun refers to the human being. Since the repelling of hardships in this world is either by a person's own strength or by the help of another, God informed us that on the Day of Resurrection both will be absent.

﴿By the sky with its return﴾. The meaning of "raj'" (return) according to the majority is rain, and it was called "raj'" as a verbal noun, because it returns each year, or because it returns to the earth. It was also said: "raj'" is the cloud that contains the rain. It was also said: it is the verbal noun of the return of the sun and the stars from one station to another.

﴿And by the earth with its cracking﴾. That is, what the earth splits open with of vegetation. It was also said: it means what is in the earth of fissures, trenches, and the like.

﴿Indeed, it is a decisive word﴾. The pronoun refers to the Qur'an, because the context of the discourse requires it. "Fasl" (decisive) means that which separates truth from falsehood, just as it is called "Furqan" (the Criterion). "Hazl" (jest) means play, that is, that it is entirely serious.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 86, verse 15–17:

﴿Indeed they are plotting a plot﴾. The pronoun refers to the disbelievers of Quraysh, and their plot is what they devised concerning the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), namely harming him and nullifying his cause. ﴿And I am planning a plan﴾. This is calling the punishment by the name of the sin, for the sake of correspondence (mushakalah) between the two actions. ﴿So give respite to the disbelievers﴾. That is, do not hasten to punish them or to invoke curses upon them. This is abrogated (mansukh) by the sword. ﴿Give them a little respite﴾. That is, a brief, small respite, meaning until their killing on the day of Badr, or until the Hereafter. He made it small because everything that is coming is near. The word ruwaydan here is an adjective (sifah) of an omitted verbal noun (masdar), and it may occur with the meaning of a command to take things easily, as in your saying: "Ruwaydan, O so-and-so." The command is repeated in His saying "give them respite," and He varied it from the word mahhil for the sake of increased calm and patience, as said by al-Zamakhshari.
